title: Countable and uncountable nouns with different meanings
subtitle: glass / a glass, art / the arts
summary: Learn the nouns whose meaning changes completely depending on whether they are used countably or uncountably.

lesson.heading: Stuff or things?
lesson.text: When we use a **countable** noun we are thinking of specific things that can be counted. When we use an **uncountable** noun we are thinking of stuff, material, or the idea of a thing in general. Some nouns can do both - with a different meaning each time.

examples.text: Be careful - there's broken **glass** on the road.
Could I have **a glass** of water, please?
There's **a fish** in that tank with beautiful markings.

lesson.heading: Same word, two meanings (1)
rows: She has beautiful red **hair**. (all of it)
There's **a hair** in my soup! (a single one)
The printer has run out of **paper**. (the material)
Did you buy **a paper** this morning? (a newspaper)
Ships made of **iron** would sink. (the metal)
Can I borrow your **iron**? My shirt is creased. (the instrument)
I love meeting **people** from different countries. (individuals)
They campaign to help indigenous **peoples**. (ethnic groups)
This shirt is made of fine **cloth**. (the material)
I need **a cloth** to wipe the table. (a piece for wiping)
Most people don't keep **wood** at home. (the material)
They walked through **a wood**. (a small forest)

lesson.heading: Same word, two meanings (2)
rows: She has little **work experience**. (knowledge or skill from doing something)
I had some interesting **experiences** on my trip. (things that happened to me)
Have you been to the modern **art** museum? (painting, drawing, sculpture)
The city has a yearly **arts** festival. (music, theatre, etc.)
They've done a lot of **work** on the project. (effort, labour)
Hamlet is one of Shakespeare's most famous **works**. (a play, book or painting)
**Time** passes very slowly if you have a boring job. (clock time)
I've seen that film three **times**. (occasions)
There was a lot of **damage** to the car. (things broken or destroyed)
She won $500,000 in **damages**. (money awarded by a court)
PLANT AND HEAVY MACHINERY CROSSING (industrial equipment)
I've bought you a house **plant**. (a botanical item)
lesson.note: Arts also names a group of university subjects such as languages or history: *he studied arts, not sciences*. And we say *we had some good times at university*, meaning experiences rather than occasions.

lesson.heading: Food and drink
lesson.text: The names of food items very often change meaning depending on whether they are countable or uncountable. The uncountable form is usually the substance; the countable form is one serving or one whole item.

examples.text: We ordered **a coffee and two teas**.

lesson.heading: pepper and a pepper

left.label: pepper (uncountable)
left.text: The grey or black spice you put on your food.
examples: Could you pass the salt and **pepper**?
She put too much **pepper** in the soup.

right.label: a pepper (countable)
right.text: The red, green or yellow vegetable.
examples: I bought **a red pepper** and two onions.
Slice the **peppers** and fry them in oil.

lesson.note: The same contrast works with onion: *a hot dog with onion* (chopped up) and *an onion* (one whole one).

lesson.heading: some or a(n)?
lesson.text: Choose **some** when you want a quantity of the material and **a/an** when you want one complete item. Getting this wrong can make a request sound very strange.

examples.note: a portion cut from the cake

lesson.text: When a dictionary marks a word both [C] and [U], read both definitions - they are often two quite different words.

exercises.prompt: Is the key noun in each sentence used countably or uncountably?

items.text: Can I borrow your iron? My shirt is creased.
Did you buy a paper this morning?
There's a hair in my soup!
Hamlet is one of Shakespeare's most famous works.
There's broken glass on the road.
The printer has run out of paper.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with the meaning it has when it is countable.

pairs.right: a painting, a play or a piece of music

exercises.prompt: You want something to drink out of. What do you say?
options: Could I have a glass, please?
Could I have some glass, please?
Could I have the glasses, please?
exercises.explanation: A glass is the container; glass is the material.

exercises.prompt: You want to press your shirt. What do you say?
options: Could I borrow an iron, please?
Could I borrow some iron, please?
exercises.explanation: An iron is the instrument; iron with no article is the metal.

exercises.prompt: You want the spice for your soup. What do you say?
options: Could I have some pepper, please?
Could I have a pepper, please?
Could I have the peppers, please?
Could I have two peppers, please?
exercises.explanation: Pepper is uncountable as a spice; a pepper is the vegetable.

exercises.prompt: How did you get that puncture in your car tyre? - I drove over some ___.
exercises.explanation: Glass as a material is uncountable, so it takes some and no plural.

exercises.prompt: Daddy, what are car tyres made of? - They're made of ___.
exercises.explanation: As a material rubber is uncountable. A rubber is what you erase pencil with.

exercises.prompt: Have you worked in a primary school before? - No, I don't have any ___ of working in a primary school.
exercises.explanation: Experience meaning skill or knowledge is uncountable; experiences are things that happened to you.

exercises.prompt: I wonder who won the general election in Sweden? - We could buy ___ and find out.
exercises.explanation: A paper is a newspaper; paper is the material you print on.

exercises.prompt: Mum, what's the Mona Lisa? - It's ___ of art by a famous Italian artist.
exercises.explanation: A work is one individual painting, book or piece of music.

exercises.statement: In the road sign PLANT AND HEAVY MACHINERY CROSSING, *plant* means large industrial equipment.
exercises.explanation: Correct - uncountable plant is machinery; a plant is the botanical kind.

exercises.statement: In 'She won $500,000 in damages', *damages* means that several things were broken.
exercises.explanation: Damages means money awarded by a court for harm caused. Damage (uncountable) is the harm itself.

exercises.answer: I had some interesting experiences during my trip to Latin America.
exercises.explanation: Countable experiences = things that happened to you.
